items.title: DMF Security: Assets & Requirements
items.text:
(c) AMWA 2026, CC Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-ND 4.0)

The Dynamic Media Facility (DMF) is primarily about Media. But as it consists of IT services and devices, security is also a matter of concern. This document aims at finding out which parts of the DMF are to be considered from a security perspective. Then which assets are to be protected according to their confidentiality ©, integrity (I) and availability (A), and as we are talking media also their state of authenticity and non-repudiation (A/NR) (see The CIA Triad and Supporting Security Properties for details). Finally security requirements for the assets are defined.

items.title: System Under Consideration {#system-under-consideration}
items.text:
The system under consideration comprises assets drawn from the EBU Dynamic Media Facility (DMF) Reference Architecture v2.0, organised as follows. A production (a Media Workload in the reference architecture) is deployed across one or more Hosts, the machines within a Cluster that run the Container Platform. Each Host executes one or more Media Functions, stateless containerised units that perform media processing (e.g. mixing, graphics, format conversion). Media Functions are granted access to Domains, which scope which Media Functions are authorised to access a given media Flow. Within a Domain, Flows carry the actual timestamped media payloads (Grains) between authorised Media Functions. Replicators are the components responsible for propagating Flows between Nodes in a Cluster.

Figure 1: System Under Consideration

These assets operate within a stated zero-trust model built on authentication / authorisation / accounting, least-privilege access, segmentation, and continuous monitoring. The reference architecture itself flags two relevant gaps: encryption of media payloads is not yet? mandated, and security across multiple Clusters remains an open topic.

items.title: Assets {#assets}
items.text:
Asset Description C I A A/NR Host Hosts run an operating system and are grouped into Clusters; Kubernetes uses the specific terminology of "Nodes" for these Hosts. A Host executes Media Functions. ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Media Workload A Media Workload consists of an organised collection of Media Functions and the flows that connect them, working together to transform inputs into a Media Product. ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Media Function A Media Function is a processing unit that performs a specific operation on media. A well-defined unit of functionality that acts on media (e.g. format conversion, mixing, colour correction, graphics rendering). Media Functions are stateless and are provisioned as one or more Containers. ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Domain The Media Exchange layer defines Domains as a mechanism to identify which Flows can be accessed by Media Functions. A mechanism defined at the Media Exchange layer to identify which Flows can be accessed by which Media Functions; in the MXL SDK, a Flow is addressed by the tuple {Host ID, Domain ID, Flow ID}, uniquely identifying a directory of memory-mapped files holding Grains. (✓) ✓ ✓ ✓ Flow(s) Audio / Video / Anc + associated metadata transported by MXL (✓) ✓ ✓ ✓ Replicator A service responsible for replicating media flows between nodes so that authorised media functions on different hosts can consume the same media. ✓ ✓ ✓ Assumed future Assets Flow Orchestration Management of media functions and flows Device and application configuration ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Production Group of Media Workloads servicing one media production. ✓ ✓ ✓ Control plane Ability to control media functions, flows, ability to orchestrate, etc ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Exposed media services Services with ports exposed to the outside of DMF (e.g. Media streams) ✓ ✓ ✓ Operational Interfaces Services communicating with external UIs and APIs ✓ ✓ ✓ Identity Identity and associated privileges of a (human) operator interacting with the system ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Logs Security and operation records; source material for SIEM and other cyber automation tools ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

items.title: Security Requirements {#security-requirements}
items.text:
• Each entity in a DMF shall have a verifiable identity.
  • Identities and credentials shall be centrally managed in a DMF.
  • Authentication and authorization are centrally managed in a DMF.
  • Flows, Domains, control, state, logs and monitoring information shall be protected against unauthorized access, modification and deletion.
  • Control actions shall be authenticated, authorized, attributable, and protected against replay.
  • Each Media Function shall check the identity and authorization of the source of requested actions
  • Configuration changes shall be validated, auditable, and reversible.
  • Credentials, connections, permissions, and retained data shall be withdrawn or disposed of when no longer required.
  • All hardware and software hosting or supporting the DMF shall be secured and hardened according to the relevant best practices.
  • High-impact operator actions shall include safeguards against human error.
  • Availability, capacity, latency, timing, and recovery requirements shall be clearly defined, and limits shall be enforced.
  • Hosts and media functions shall be protected against Denial of Service, including resource exhaustion.
  • Failures or degradation of functionality and security-relevant changes in a DMF shall be detectable, allowing triggering automated or operator response.
  • Required security and operational events shall be logged, identifying their source and relevant subject using verifiable identities. Logs shall contain sufficient context and accurate timestamps to support correlation and investigation but no sensitive information.
  • Log collection, transport, storage, and retrieval shall meet defined availability and retention needs.
  • Changes to logging and retention arrangements shall be authorized, validated, and auditable.
  • Media Workload resources and relationships shall be isolated from other , non-related Media Workloadsproductions according to risk.
  • Critical functions and flows shall have defined continuity and recovery arrangements.

items.title: The CIA Triad and Supporting Security Properties {#the-cia-triad-and-supporting-security-properties}
items.text:
# Property Description C Confidentiality Preserving authorised restrictions on information access and disclosure, including protecting personal privacy and proprietary information. I Integrity Guarding against improper information modification or destruction, including ensuring authenticity and non-repudiation. A Availability Ensuring timely[^1] and reliable access to and use of information. A/NR Authenticity The assurance that an entity, user, system, or data is genuine and has not been impersonated or falsified. Non-repudiation The assurance that the origin and integrity of data or an action can be proven, preventing an individual or entity from falsely denying having performed that action.
